bib.title: The harm of class imbalance corrections for risk prediction models: illustration and simulation using logistic regression

read.skipped: Tables S3-S8 were read for structure and selected rows only, not every cell.

question: How do random undersampling, random oversampling and SMOTE affect discrimination, calibration and classification of standard and ridge logistic regression?
hypothesis: Imbalance correction distorts calibration by inflating probabilities, and shifting the probability threshold has a similar effect on sensitivity and specificity as correction.
contributions: Simulation of 24 scenarios plus an ovarian cancer case study showing correction yields miscalibration without AUROC gain
Shows threshold shifting matches correction's classification effect

method.summary: Standard (SLR) and ridge logistic regression were trained on uncorrected, RUS, ROS and SMOTE data, in a Monte Carlo simulation and in a real ovarian tumour dataset, and compared on AUROC, calibration intercept and slope, sensitivity, specificity and Net Benefit. Corrected models were also recalibrated by an intercept-only offset model.

datasets.name: IOTA ovarian tumour data (3 waves 1999-2005, 2005-2007, 2009-2012)
datasets.source: International Ovarian Tumor Analysis study; ethics approval S64709 KU Leuven; operated patients only, borderline counted malignant
datasets.preprocessing: predictors age, max lesion diameter (mm), papillary structures (0-4); continuous predictors as restricted cubic splines with 3 knots

datasets.name: Simulated data
datasets.size: train N 2500 or 5000; test N=100,000 per scenario
datasets.split: 24 scenarios: N x p (3,6,12,24) x event fraction (0.3,0.1,0.01); 2000 runs each, new training set per run
datasets.source: multivariate standard normal predictors, zero correlation, equal strength, true c-statistic about 0.75
datasets.preprocessing: coefficients found numerically (BFGS via optim, median of 20 fits, repeated on 20 datasets of N=1e5); datasets with separation (apparent AUROC=1) or one class removed

other.lambda: grid of 251 values between 0 and 64, nonzero values equidistant on log scale, tuned by 10-fold CV on deviance; leave-one-out CV if fewer than 8 events or non-events

training.objective: maximum likelihood (SLR); penalised log-likelihood l(a,b) - lambda * sum b_j^2 (Ridge)
training.seeds: 2000 simulation runs per scenario; no seed value stated

other.RUS: discard random majority cases until majority equals minority size
other.ROS: resample minority with replacement until equal to majority size
other.SMOTE: k=5 nearest minority neighbours, difference times random number in (0,1) added to minority case; k set to events minus 1 if fewer than 6 events
other.recalibration: intercept-only logistic model on the development dataset with the logit of the initial model's estimated probability as offset: logit(pi_recalibrated) = a + logit(pi_hat); applied to RUS/ROS/SMOTE models (6 extra models)

inference.samples: 2000 simulation runs per scenario; one test set per scenario

parameters.thresholds: 0.5 default; for uncorrected models also threshold equal to event fraction (case study 0.192 = 518/2695)

metrics.name: AUROC (c statistic)
metrics.definition: probability a random event case gets higher risk than a random non-event

metrics.name: Calibration intercept
metrics.definition: a in logit(pi_i)=a+LP with LP as offset (slope fixed at 1); <0 means overestimation

metrics.name: Calibration slope
metrics.definition: b in logit(pi_i)=a+b*LP; <1 means too extreme

baselines: Uncorrected with threshold shifted to event fraction
eval.protocol: Primary metric is calibration intercept; simulation follows ADEMP; medians and IQRs over 2000 runs; case study reports 95% CIs on one test set.

availability.data: IOTA data not stated to be public; ethics approval for secondary use only

results.claim: Imbalance correction (RUS, ROS, SMOTE) never gave a higher median AUROC than uncorrected training data; RUS was often lower.
results.setup: Monte Carlo simulation, 24 scenarios (N 2500/5000, p 3/6/12/24, event fraction 0.3/0.1/0.01), 2000 runs each, SLR and Ridge, true c-statistic about 0.75, test set N=100,000
results.quote: The median AUROC of models trained on unadjusted data was never lower than the median AUROC of models after RUS, ROS, or SMOTE.

results.claim: Worst AUROC gap: SLR with 24 predictors, N=2500, 1% events: uncorrected 0.69 vs RUS 0.59 (ROS and SMOTE 0.68).
results.setup: Monte Carlo simulation, 24 scenarios (N 2500/5000, p 3/6/12/24, event fraction 0.3/0.1/0.01), 2000 runs each, SLR and Ridge, true c-statistic about 0.75, test set N=100,000; scenario 4
results.table: Table S3, scenario 4 (EF 0.01, N 2500, p 24), SLR columns Uncorrected 0.69 (0.67;0.70) vs RUS 0.59 (0.56;0.62)

results.claim: RUS lowers AUROC more when event fraction is lower, training set smaller and predictors more numerous.
results.setup: Monte Carlo simulation, 24 scenarios (N 2500/5000, p 3/6/12/24, event fraction 0.3/0.1/0.01), 2000 runs each, SLR and Ridge, true c-statistic about 0.75, test set N=100,000
results.quote: For RUS, the median AUROC was often lower, with larger differences when event fraction was lower, training set size was lower, and number of predictors was higher.

results.claim: Models trained on uncorrected data had median calibration intercepts near zero.
results.setup: Monte Carlo simulation, 24 scenarios (N 2500/5000, p 3/6/12/24, event fraction 0.3/0.1/0.01), 2000 runs each, SLR and Ridge, true c-statistic about 0.75, test set N=100,000
results.quote: Models trained on unadjusted data had median calibration intercepts between -0.05 and 0.03.

results.claim: Imbalance correction gave median calibration intercept of -4.5 or lower at 1% event fraction.
results.setup: Monte Carlo simulation, 24 scenarios (N 2500/5000, p 3/6/12/24, event fraction 0.3/0.1/0.01), 2000 runs each, SLR and Ridge, true c-statistic about 0.75, test set N=100,000; 1% event fraction (-2.1 at 10%, -0.7 at 30%)
results.quote: Imbalance correction methods had median calibration intercepts of -4.5 or lower for scenarios with a 1% event fraction, -2.1 or lower for scenarios with a 10% event fraction, and -0.7 or lower for scenarios with a 30% event fraction.

results.claim: Intercept-only logistic recalibration restored median calibration intercepts to between -0.07 and 0.03.
results.setup: Monte Carlo simulation, 24 scenarios (N 2500/5000, p 3/6/12/24, event fraction 0.3/0.1/0.01), 2000 runs each, SLR and Ridge, true c-statistic about 0.75, test set N=100,000; recalibration of RUS/ROS/SMOTE models; exception SLR after RUS with 1% events, N=2500, p=24 (only 25 events and 25 non-events on average, no convergence)
results.note: Methods say the recalibration model is fitted on the development dataset; Results say 'Using the original (imbalanced) data'. Reading: the original uncorrected training data.
results.quote: recalibration improved median calibration intercepts to values between -0.07 and 0.03

results.claim: Ovarian case study: AUROC 0.79 to 0.80 for all algorithm and correction combinations.
results.setup: IOTA data, 3369 premenopausal patients, 658 malignant (20%); train 2695 (518 events), test 674 (140 events); predictors age, lesion diameter, papillary structures; 3-knot restricted cubic splines; SLR and Ridge
results.quote: with average AUROC of 0.79 to 0.80 (Table S2)

results.claim: Ovarian case study: calibration intercept 0.06 (SLR) and 0.05 (Ridge) uncorrected, versus -1.32 to -1.50 after correction.
results.setup: IOTA ovarian case study, test set n=674
results.quote: these were 0.06 (95% CI -0.16 to 0.26) for SLR and 0.05 (-0.16 to 0.26) for Ridge on training data without imbalance correction

results.claim: Ovarian: at threshold 0.5 uncorrected models had sensitivity 31% (SLR), 29% (Ridge) and specificity 96%.
results.quote: specificity (96% for SLR and Ridge) was clearly higher than sensitivity (31% for SLR, 29% for Ridge)

results.claim: Ovarian: corrected models at threshold 0.5 gave sensitivities 69-75% and specificities 74-78%.
results.setup: IOTA ovarian case study; the sentence covers corrected models at 0.5 and uncorrected models at the shifted threshold
results.note: Text says 'sensitivity increased and specificity increased', evidently a slip for 'decreased'. Table S2: corrected models at 0.5 sens 69-71, spec 74-78.

results.claim: Ovarian: shifting the threshold to 0.192 (training prevalence 518/2695) on uncorrected SLR gave sensitivity 71% and specificity 76%, accuracy 75%.
results.setup: IOTA ovarian case study, uncorrected models, test n=674
results.note: Corrected models are Nc (not computed) at 0.192.
results.table: Table S2, SLR rows Sensitivity t=0.192 = 71, Specificity t=0.192 = 76, Accuracy t=0.192 = 75; Ridge 70 / 76 / 75

results.claim: Ovarian: calibration slope 0.99 (SLR) and 1.03 (Ridge) uncorrected; lowest after RUS (0.85 SLR, 0.93 Ridge).
results.quote: (0.99 for SLR, 1.03 for Ridge) and lowest (i.e. worst) for models after RUS (0.85 for SLR, 0.93 for Ridge)

results.claim: Ovarian: Net Benefit of corrected models was negative at thresholds of 0.3 or higher.
results.setup: IOTA ovarian case study, decision curve (Figure 2)
results.quote: even to the extent that the Net Benefit was negative when using a probability threshold of 0.3 or higher to select individuals for treatment

results.claim: At 1% event fraction with threshold 0.5, uncorrected models had median sensitivity 0% and specificity 100%.
results.setup: Monte Carlo simulation, 24 scenarios (N 2500/5000, p 3/6/12/24, event fraction 0.3/0.1/0.01), 2000 runs each, SLR and Ridge, true c-statistic about 0.75, test set N=100,000; uncorrected, threshold 0.5
results.quote: resulted in median sensitivities of 0% and median specificities of 100% when the true event fraction was 1%

results.claim: Resampling methods, and shifting the threshold, both balance sensitivity and specificity.
results.setup: Monte Carlo simulation, 24 scenarios (N 2500/5000, p 3/6/12/24, event fraction 0.3/0.1/0.01), 2000 runs each, SLR and Ridge, true c-statistic about 0.75, test set N=100,000
results.quote: specificity were obtained by either using imbalance correction methods or shifting the probability threshold

results.claim: SMOTE and to a lesser extent ROS give median calibration slopes below 1 (too extreme probabilities); SLR after RUS overfits more.
results.setup: Monte Carlo simulation, 24 scenarios (N 2500/5000, p 3/6/12/24, event fraction 0.3/0.1/0.01), 2000 runs each, SLR and Ridge, true c-statistic about 0.75, test set N=100,000
results.quote: The use of SMOTE, and to a lesser extent ROS, resulted probability estimates that were too extreme as evidenced by median calibration slopes below 1

results.claim: Headline conclusion: outcome imbalance is not a problem in itself; correction may worsen performance.
results.setup: Abstract, standard and ridge logistic regression only
results.quote: Our study shows that outcome imbalance is not a problem in itself, and that imbalance correction may even worsen model performance.

limits: Only standard and ridge logistic regression were tested; Random Forest, SVM and neural networks are left for follow-up
Other corrections (weighting, cost-sensitive learning, variants of RUS/ROS/SMOTE) not tested
Authors anticipate miscalibration will persist for other models and techniques unless recalibrated, but this was not tested
Simulation uses uncorrelated predictors of equal strength and one true c-statistic of about 0.75
Case study has a single 4:1 split with moderate imbalance (20%)
Preprint with no venue printed; main text 3148 words
